lead: Two formulas put a ceiling on how many bits per second a link can carry. Nyquist gives the limit when the channel has no noise and the sender uses a fixed number of signal levels. Shannon gives the limit when noise is present, which every real wire, fibre and radio link has. Engineers use both before buying hardware: they show whether extra bandwidth, extra signal power or more signal levels will raise the rate. The same sums decide a telephone modem, a DSL line and a Wi-Fi channel.
prereq: You need 2.1 for bandwidth and frequency, and 2.2 for signal-to-noise ratio.

blocks.text: In an ideal noiseless low-pass channel of bandwidth B hertz, the receiver can take 2B independent samples per second. This is the sampling result behind the Nyquist rate: a signal whose highest frequency is B needs at least 2B samples per second to be reconstructed. Each sample may take one of L distinct signal levels. One sample then carries log₂ L bits, because log₂ L is the number of binary choices needed to name one of L levels.

blocks.where: R_N is the maximum bit rate in bit/s; B is the channel bandwidth in hertz; L is the number of signal levels used per sample.

blocks.text: With L = 2, each sample carries one bit, so the rate is 2B bit/s. With L = 8, each sample carries three bits, so the rate is 6B. Doubling B doubles the rate. Doubling L adds exactly one bit per sample, because log₂(2L) = log₂ L + 1. This is a sampling argument, not a law of nature: it assumes no noise and perfect timing, and it assumes the receiver can tell all L levels apart. It does not say that a noisy channel can do so.
Shannon capacity is the highest error-free bit rate a real channel can support. For a channel of bandwidth B hertz with average signal power S and average noise power N,

blocks.where: C is the capacity in bit/s; B is the bandwidth in hertz; S/N is the signal-to-noise power ratio, a unitless number.

blocks.text: Here S/N is a power ratio, never the decibel figure. If a meter shows SNR<sub>dB</sub>, convert it: SNR<sub>dB</sub> = 10 log₁₀(S/N), so S/N = 10^(SNR<sub>dB</sub>/10). For example, 30 dB means S/N = 10^3 = 1000; 35 dB means about 3162. Put 3162 into the formula, not 35. To compute the base-2 logarithm by hand, use log₂ X = log₁₀ X ÷ 0.301. Shannon capacity rises linearly with B. It also rises with S/N, but only as a logarithm, so a large power increase gives a small rate increase. Capacity is an upper bound; no real system exceeds it.

sections.h3: Choosing levels: where the two meet

blocks.text: Set the Nyquist rate equal to Shannon capacity and solve for L:

blocks.where: The left side is the Nyquist rate for L levels; the right side is Shannon capacity. Divide both sides by B.

blocks.text: Divide by B: 2 log₂ L = log₂(1 + S/N). So log₂ L² = log₂(1 + S/N), which gives L = √(1 + S/N). That L is the largest number of levels that still reaches the Shannon limit. Use more levels and noise makes neighbours look alike; use fewer and the link runs below capacity. The two formulas therefore agree only when the level count is chosen from the measured S/N.

On a voice-band telephone channel B ≈ 3 kHz and SNR ≈ 35 dB. Shannon gives about 35 kbit/s. Practical analog voice-band modems stalled near that figure: with B = 3 kHz and 35 dB, about 56 levels is the useful ceiling. To go faster, the link needs more bandwidth or a better S/N. How bits are actually mapped to levels is covered in 2.6.

figure.caption: Nyquist for eight levels rises at 6 kbit/s per kHz. Shannon for 35 dB rises at about 11.6 kbit/s per kHz, so the real-channel ceiling is higher here.

spec.aria: Two rising straight lines: the eight-level Nyquist rate is 6 kbit/s per kHz, the 35 dB Shannon capacity is about 11.6 kbit/s per kHz.

examples.question: A telephone channel has bandwidth B = 3 kHz and SNR<sub>dB</sub> = 35 dB. (a) Find the Shannon capacity in kbit/s. (b) Find the Nyquist bit rate for L = 8 levels. (c) Find the level count L that would just reach the Shannon capacity.
steps: Convert the decibel figure: S/N = 10^(35/10) = 10^3.5 = 3162.3, about 3162.
Nyquist for L = 8: R = 2 × 3000 × log₂ 8 = 6000 × 3 = 18,000 bit/s = 18.0 kbit/s.
Levels at the Shannon limit: L = √(1 + 3162.3) = √3163.3 ≈ 56.2. Since 57 levels would exceed capacity, use at most 56 whole levels.
examples.answer: Shannon capacity is about 34.9 kbit/s, the 8-level Nyquist rate is 18.0 kbit/s, and the Shannon limit needs about 56.2 levels; to meet the limit, round down to 56 whole levels.
examples.check:
import math
B = 3000.0
snr_db = 35.0
snr = 10**(snr_db/10)
C = B * math.log2(1 + snr)
R = 2 * B * math.log2(8)
L = math.sqrt(1 + snr)
print(f"{C/1000:.1f}")
print(f"{R/1000:.1f}")
print(f"{L:.1f}")

traps: Putting SNR<sub>dB</sub> = 35 straight into Shannon. The formula needs S/N = 3162, a power ratio. Convert first.
Forgetting the factor 2 in the Nyquist formula, or using B in kHz while the formula expects hertz. 3 kHz must be 3000 Hz.
Treating log₂ L as L. With 8 levels each sample carries 3 bits, not 8 bits.
Calling the Nyquist result a channel capacity. It is the maximum rate for the chosen L on a noiseless channel; Shannon capacity is the real-channel ceiling.
Using the level formula L = √(1 + S/N) as bits per symbol. Bits per symbol is log₂ L.

quiz.q: State the Nyquist bit-rate formula and define B and L.
quiz.a: R_N = 2 × B × log₂ L; B is bandwidth in hertz and L is the number of signal levels.

quiz.q: Why does the Nyquist formula contain 2B rather than B?
quiz.a: An ideal low-pass channel of bandwidth B needs at least 2B samples per second by the sampling theorem; each sample carries log₂ L bits.

quiz.q: A noiseless channel has B = 4 kHz and L = 16. Find the Nyquist bit rate.
A channel has B = 1 MHz and SNR<sub>dB</sub> = 20 dB. Find Shannon capacity.
Why can adding more signal levels stop increasing the reliable bit rate?
quiz.a: Noise separates the levels; beyond L ≈ √(1 + S/N) adjacent levels overlap at the receiver, so errors rise and the extra levels cannot be used reliably.

quiz.q: For B = 3 kHz and SNR<sub>dB</sub> = 35 dB, estimate the largest useful L. Explain whether to round up or down for a whole number of levels.
quiz.a: S/N ≈ 3162; L ≈ √3163 ≈ 56.2. Whole levels must not push the Nyquist rate above Shannon, so round down: 56 levels is the largest reliable count (56 levels give 2 × 3000 × log₂56 ≈ 34.8 kbit/s, just under the 34.9 kbit/s capacity).

quiz.q: Convert SNR<sub>dB</sub> = 30 dB to S/N and explain what the number means.
quiz.a: S/N = 10^(30/10) = 1000. Signal power is 1000 times noise power.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every modern radio chooses its level count from the measured S/N: Wi-Fi, 4G and 5G change modulation and coding as the channel changes. The same capacity sums guide DSL and optical link design. Shannon's limit is a ceiling, not a recipe; real systems approach it with coding such as turbo and LDPC codes. Search for Shannon-Hartley theorem, adaptive modulation and coding, and channel capacity.
